content: 1. To establish the presence of a chemical in drinking water as a concern, one of the following criteria must be met: credible evidence of its occurrence in drinking water combined with evidence of actual or potential toxicity; significant international concern regarding the chemical; or its inclusion or consideration for inclusion in the WHO Pesticide Evaluation Scheme (WHOPES), which evaluates pesticides used for public health purposes, including those applied directly to drinking water for controlling disease vectors. 2. Guideline values are derived for many chemical constituents of drinking water. These values represent concentrations that do not pose significant health risks over a lifetime of consumption. In some cases, provisional guideline values are set at concentrations achievable through practical treatment methods or laboratory analysis, even if these values exceed calculated health-based values. 3. For certain chemicals, no formal guideline value is proposed because their occurrence is consistently at concentrations well below levels of health concern. Establishing formal guideline values for such substances could lead to unnecessary incorporation into national standards by some Member States. 4. To assist Member States in hazard identification during the development of a Water Safety Plan (WSP), health-based values are determined for chemicals that may be found in drinking water or source water. Additionally, health-based values for acute exposures are being developed for substances that may be involved in emergency situations, such as spills into surface water sources. 5. When deriving guideline values, data on the proportion of total daily intake typically ingested through drinking water are used. This is based on mean levels in food, water, consumer products, soil, and air, or on intake estimates derived from the physical and chemical properties of the substances. It is important to quantify exposures from both food and water whenever possible. 6. For most contaminants, exposure data from various sources, such as food and drinking water, are primarily available from developed countries. The default allocation of total daily intake to drinking water is set at 20%, reflecting a reasonable level of exposure while remaining protective. This allocation has been revised from a previous value of 10%, which was deemed overly conservative. 7. In cases where water is the primary or sole source of exposure, such as for certain disinfection by-products (DBPs), the allocation may be as high as 80%, allowing for some exposure from other sources. For pesticides, even when food exposure data suggest minimal exposure, the default allocation of 20% is used to account for potential higher exposure in developing countries. 8. The Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) or Tolerable Daily Intake (TDI) is used to derive guideline values, typically rounded to one significant figure to reflect uncertainties in experimental data, exposure assumptions, and selected uncertainty factors. 9. Small exceedances of guideline values for short periods are not typically considered a health emergency. However, in the event of a spill, a higher allocation of the ADI to drinking water may be justified. Efforts should be made to keep pesticide concentrations in water as low as possible and not allow them to increase up to the guideline value. 10. Effective treatment of pharmaceuticals in drinking water depends on the physicochemical properties of the specific compounds. Conventional treatment processes are generally less effective than advanced treatment processes for removing many organic compounds, particularly those that are highly water-soluble. 11. The guideline value for nitrate in drinking water is set at 50 mg/L (as nitrate ion) to protect the most sensitive subpopulation, bottle-fed infants, from adverse health effects such as methemoglobinemia and thyroid effects. Authorities should ensure that water used for bottle-fed infants is microbiologically safe, especially when nitrate concentrations are near or above the guideline value. 12. Acute Reference Doses (ARfDs) are derived for chemicals used in significant quantities and involved in emergencies, such as spills into surface water sources. These ARfDs are protective of the entire population, including the embryo or fetus, and are based on toxicological endpoints relevant to single or short-term exposures. 13. When suitable single-dose or short-term data are unavailable, endpoints from repeated-dose toxicity studies may be used, though this approach is more conservative. In emergencies, if an ARfD is not available but a guideline value or health-based value exists, a pragmatic approach may allocate a higher proportion of the ADI or TDI to drinking water for a short period. 14. Turbidity in water, caused by suspended particles such as sediments, plant debris, and microorganisms, reduces water clarity. Turbidity can result from poor source water quality, inadequate treatment, or disturbances in distribution systems. It is detectable instrumentally below 4 NTU and visually at 4 NTU or above.
